blocks.p: But now, to see how things fell out: one of the prisoners, Incredulity by name, broke out of prison in the time between the sentence and the execution, and made his escape. He got clean away from Mansoul and lay lurking in whatever holes and corners he could find, waiting for another chance to do the town some mischief for the way they had handled him.

When Mr. Trueman the jailer found that he had lost his prisoner, he was in great distress, because that prisoner was, so to speak, the very worst of the whole gang. So first he went and told the Lord Mayor, Mr. Recorder, and Lord Willbewill, and got an order from them to search the whole town for him. The order was given and the search was made, but no such man was now to be found anywhere in Mansoul.

All that could be learned was that he had lurked a while about the outside of the town, and that here and there someone had caught a glimpse of him as he made his escape. One or two also declared that they had seen him outside the town, going at a great pace across the plain. And after he was quite gone, a certain Mr. Did-see affirmed that he had roamed through dry places until he met with his friend Diabolus; and where should they meet but on Hell-gate Hill.
But oh, what a lamentable story the old gentleman told Diabolus about the sad change Emmanuel had made in Mansoul!

He told him first how Mansoul, after some delays, had received a general pardon from Emmanuel’s hand; how they had invited him into the town and given him the castle for his own; how they had called in his soldiers and competed over who should quarter the most of them; and how they had welcomed him with tambourine, song, and dance.

“But what grieves me most of all,” said Incredulity, “is that he has pulled down your image, father, and set up his own, and pulled down your officers and set up his own. Yes, and Willbewill, that rebel, who you would have thought would never turn from us, is now in as great favor with Emmanuel as ever he was with you. On top of all this, Willbewill has received a special commission from his master to search out, arrest, and put to death every Diabolonian of every kind he finds in Mansoul; and he has already taken eight of my lord’s most trusted friends there and put them in prison. More than that, my lord, and it grieves me to say it, they have all been tried and condemned, and I fear by now executed in Mansoul. I told my lord of eight; I myself was the ninth, and I would surely have drunk from the same cup, except that by cunning, as you see, I have escaped them.”

When Diabolus had heard this lamentable story, he yelled and snuffed up the wind like a dragon, and made the sky look dark with his roaring. He swore, too, that he would try to be revenged on Mansoul for this. So he and his old friend Incredulity agreed to enter into a great consultation about how they might win Mansoul back.

Now before this time, the day had come on which the prisoners in Mansoul were to be executed. So they were brought to the cross, and that by Mansoul itself, in a most solemn manner; for the Prince had said it must be done by the town’s own hand.

“So that I may see,” he said, “how ready my now redeemed Mansoul is to keep my word and do my commandments, and so that I may bless Mansoul for doing this deed. Proof of sincerity pleases me well. Let Mansoul, therefore, be the first to lay their hands on these Diabolonians to destroy them.”

So the town of Mansoul put them to death, as their Prince had said. But when the prisoners were brought to the cross to die, you would hardly believe what troublesome work Mansoul had of it. For the men knew they must die, and every one of them had a relentless hatred of Mansoul in his heart; so what did they do but take courage at the cross and fight back against the men of the town? The men of Mansoul were forced to cry out to the captains and soldiers for help. Now the great Shaddai had a Secretary in the town, who was a great lover of the men of Mansoul, and he was at the place of execution too. Hearing them cry out against the struggling and unruliness of the prisoners, he rose from his place and came and put his hands on the hands of the men of Mansoul. And so they crucified the Diabolonians who had been a plague, a grief, and an offense to the town of Mansoul.

When this good work was done, the Prince came down to see them, to visit them, to speak comfortably to the men of Mansoul, and to strengthen their hands for such work. He told them that by this act of theirs he had tested them, and had found them to be lovers of his person, keepers of his laws, and men who had regard for his honor. And to show them that they would not be the losers by it, nor their town weakened by the loss of those men, he said he would make them another captain, and one of their own people; and that this captain should command a thousand men, for the good of the now flourishing town.

So he called to him one whose name was Waiting, and told him, “Go quickly up to the castle gate and ask there for a Mr. Experience, who serves that noble captain, Captain Credence, and tell him to come here to me.”
So the messenger went and did as he was told. The young gentleman was at that moment watching the captain train and muster his men in the castle yard.
“Sir,” Mr. Waiting said to him, “the Prince wants you to come down to his Highness at once.”

So he brought him down to Emmanuel, and he came and bowed low before him. Now the men of the town knew Mr. Experience well, for he was born and raised in Mansoul. They knew him to be a man of good conduct and courage, and wise in his dealings; he was also handsome, well-spoken, and very successful in whatever he undertook.
So the hearts of the townspeople were carried away with joy when they saw that the Prince himself was so taken with Mr. Experience that he meant to make him captain over a band of men.
With one accord they bowed the knee before Emmanuel and shouted, “Long live Emmanuel forever!”
Then the Prince said to Mr. Experience, “I have thought it good to give you a place of trust and honor in this my town of Mansoul.” And the young man bowed his head and worshiped.
“It is this,” said Emmanuel: “that you shall be a captain, a captain over a thousand men in my beloved town of Mansoul.”
“Long live the King!” said the captain.

So the Prince at once gave orders to the King’s Secretary to draw up a commission for Mr. Experience, making him a captain over a thousand men. “And let it be brought to me,” he said, “so that I may set my seal to it.” It was done as he commanded: the commission was drawn up and brought to Emmanuel, and he sealed it. Then he sent it away to the captain by the hand of Mr. Waiting.

As soon as the captain had received his commission, he sounded his trumpet for volunteers, and young men came to him quickly; yes, the greatest and chief men of the town sent their sons to be enlisted under his command. So Captain Experience came under Emmanuel’s command, for the good of Mansoul. He had for his lieutenant a Mr. Skilful, and for his cornet, the officer who carried the colors, a Mr. Memory. His lower officers I need not name. His colors were the white colors, for the town of Mansoul, and his escutcheon, the emblem on his shield, was the dead lion and the dead bear. Then the Prince went back again to his royal palace.

Once he was back, the elders of Mansoul, the Lord Mayor, the Recorder, and Lord Willbewill, went to congratulate him, and especially to thank him for the love, care, and tender compassion he had shown to his ever-indebted town of Mansoul. So after a while, and some sweet fellowship between them, the townsmen solemnly finished their ceremony and returned to their places.

At this time Emmanuel also appointed them a day on which he would renew their charter; yes, renew it and enlarge it, mending several faults in it, so that Mansoul’s yoke might be easier still. And this he did unasked, purely out of his own generosity and noble mind. When he had sent for their old charter and looked it over, he laid it aside and said, “Now what is decaying and growing old is ready to vanish away.” [Heb. 8:13] He said moreover, “The town of Mansoul shall have another: a better one, a new one, far more steady and firm.” Here is a summary of it:
I, Emmanuel, Prince of Peace, and a great lover of the town of Mansoul, in the name of my Father and out of my own mercy, give, grant, and bequeath to my beloved town of Mansoul:
1. Free, full, and everlasting forgiveness of all wrongs, injuries, and offenses they have done against my Father, against me, against their neighbor, or against themselves.
2. I give them the holy law and my testament, with all that they contain, for their everlasting comfort and consolation.
3. I also give them a share of the very same grace and goodness that lives in my Father’s heart and in mine.

4. I give, grant, and freely bestow on them the world and everything in it, for their good; and they shall have such power over these things as agrees with my Father’s honor, my glory, and their comfort. Yes, I grant them the benefits of life and of death, of things present and of things to come. No other city, town, or corporation shall have this privilege, but my Mansoul only.

5. I give and grant them leave and free access to me in my palace at all times, whether my palace above or below, to make their needs known to me there; and I give them, moreover, a promise that I will hear them and set right all their grievances.

6. I give and grant to the town of Mansoul, and invest it with, full power and authority to seek out, seize, enslave, and destroy every Diabolonian of every kind who at any time, from anywhere, shall be found straggling in or about the town of Mansoul.

7. I further grant to my beloved town of Mansoul authority not to allow any foreigner or stranger, or their offspring, to be free in and of the blessed town of Mansoul, or to share in its excellent privileges. All the grants, privileges, and immunities I bestow on the famous town of Mansoul shall be for its old natives and true inhabitants; for them, I say, and for their rightful offspring after them.
But all Diabolonians, of whatever sort, birth, country, or kingdom, shall be barred from any share in them.

When the town of Mansoul had received their gracious charter from Emmanuel’s hand (and the charter itself is infinitely larger than this lean summary sets before you), they carried it to the marketplace, and there Mr. Recorder read it in the presence of all the people. Then it was carried back to the castle gates and handsomely engraved on the doors, inlaid in letters of gold, so that all the people of Mansoul might always have it in view, or go where they could see what a blessed freedom their Prince had bestowed on them; so that their joy might increase and their love to their great and good Emmanuel be renewed.

But what joy, what comfort, what consolation, do you think, now filled the hearts of the men of Mansoul! The bells rang, the musicians played, the people danced, the captains shouted, the colors waved in the wind, and the silver trumpets sounded; and the Diabolonians were glad now to hide their heads, for they looked like men long dead.

When this was over, the Prince sent again for the elders of Mansoul and talked with them about a ministry he intended to establish among them: a ministry that might open things to them, and instruct them in whatever concerned their present and their future state.
“For,” he said, “left to yourselves, unless you have teachers and guides, you will not be able to know my Father’s will; and if you do not know it, you certainly will not do it.”

When the elders brought this news to the people, the whole town came running together (for it pleased them well, as everything the Prince now did pleased the people), and all with one consent begged his Majesty to establish at once such a ministry among them as might teach them both law and judgment, statute and commandment, so that they might be instructed in all good and wholesome things. He told them he would grant their request, and would establish two among them: one from his Father’s court, and one a native of Mansoul.

“The one from the court,” he said, “is a person of no less rank and dignity than my Father and I. He is the Lord Chief Secretary of my Father’s house; for he is, and always has been, the one who dictates all my Father’s laws, a person perfectly skilled in all mysteries and in the knowledge of mysteries, as my Father is, and as I am myself. Indeed, he is one with us in nature, and one with us too in loving the town of Mansoul, in being faithful to it, and in its eternal concerns.

“And this is he who must be your chief teacher; for it is he, and he alone, who can teach you clearly in all high and supernatural things. He, and he alone, knows the ways and methods of my Father at court; no one can show as he can how my Father’s heart is toward Mansoul at all times, in all things, on all occasions. For as no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him, so no one knows the things of my Father except this his high and mighty Secretary. [1 Cor. 2:11] Nor can anyone tell Mansoul as he can how and what they must do to keep themselves in my Father’s love. He is also the one who can bring lost things back to your remembrance, and tell you things to come. This teacher, therefore, must of necessity have first place, both in your affections and in your judgment, above your other teacher. His personal dignity, the excellence of his teaching, and the great skill he has in helping you frame petitions to my Father, for your help and to his pleasure, must lay obligations on you to love him, to fear him, and to take care that you do not grieve him.

“This person can put life and vigor into all he says; yes, and he can put it into your hearts too. This person can make seers of you, and can make you tell what shall be hereafter. Through this person you must frame all your petitions to my Father and to me; and without first getting his advice and counsel, let nothing come into the town or castle of Mansoul, for that may offend and grieve this noble person.

“Take care, I say, that you do not grieve this minister; for if you do, he may fight against you. And should you ever move him to set himself against you in battle array, that will distress you more than if twelve legions were sent from my Father’s court to make war on you.

“But, as I said, if you will listen to him and love him; if you will devote yourselves to his teaching, and seek to talk with him and keep up fellowship with him, you will find him ten times better than the whole world could be to anyone. Yes, he will pour out my Father’s love in your hearts, and Mansoul will be the wisest and most blessed of all peoples.”

Then the Prince called to him the old gentleman who had formerly been the Recorder of Mansoul, Mr. Conscience by name. He told him that since he was well skilled in the law and government of the town, and was also well-spoken, and could aptly deliver his Master’s will to them in all earthly and domestic matters, he would make him a minister as well to the goodly town of Mansoul, in all its laws, statutes, and judgments.

“But you must,” said the Prince, “confine yourself to teaching moral virtues, and civil and natural duties. You must not presume to set yourself up as a revealer of those high and supernatural mysteries that are kept close in the heart of Shaddai, my Father; for no one knows those things, and no one can reveal them, except my Father’s Secretary.

“You are a native of the town of Mansoul, but the Lord Secretary is a native with my Father. So, as you have knowledge of the laws and customs of the corporation, he has knowledge of the things and the will of my Father.

“Therefore, Mr. Conscience, although I have made you a minister and a preacher to the town of Mansoul, yet in the things that the Lord Secretary knows, and shall teach to this people, you must be his scholar and a learner, just as the rest of Mansoul are.

“In all high and supernatural things, then, you must go to him for information and knowledge; for though there is a spirit in man, it is this person’s inspiration that must give him understanding. [Job 32:8] So, my old Recorder, keep low and be humble, and remember that the Diabolonians who did not keep their first charge, but left their own standing, are now made prisoners in the pit. Be content, therefore, with your station.

“I have made you my Father’s deputy on earth in the things I have just mentioned. Take power to teach them to Mansoul; yes, and to enforce them with whips and chastisements, if they will not willingly listen and do what you command.

“And, my old Recorder, because you are old, and made feeble by many abuses, I give you leave and license to go whenever you like to my fountain, my conduit, and to drink freely there of the blood of my grape; for my conduit always runs with wine. By doing so you will drive out of your heart and stomach all foul, gross, and harmful humors. It will also brighten your eyes, and strengthen your memory to receive and keep all that the King’s most noble Secretary teaches.”

When the Prince had in this way put Mr. Conscience, the Recorder that once was, into the office of minister to Mansoul, and the man had thankfully accepted it, Emmanuel addressed a particular speech to the townspeople themselves.

“See,” said the Prince to Mansoul, “my love and care for you. To all that is past I have added this mercy: I have appointed you preachers. The most noble Secretary is to teach you in all high and lofty mysteries; and this gentleman,” pointing to Mr. Conscience, “is to teach you in all things human and domestic, for that is where his work lies. By what I have said he is not forbidden to tell Mansoul anything he has heard and received from the mouth of the Lord High Secretary; only he must not presume to set himself up as a revealer of those high mysteries himself. For opening them up and making them known to Mansoul lies only in the power, authority, and skill of the Lord High Secretary himself. He may talk of them, and so may the rest of the town of Mansoul; yes, and as occasion gives them opportunity, they may press them on one another for the benefit of the whole. These things, then, I would have you observe and do, for it is for your life, and the lengthening of your days.

“And one thing more, to my beloved Mr. Conscience and to all the town of Mansoul. You must not rest in or lean on anything he has in his commission to teach you, as far as your trust and hope for the next world are concerned. (The next world, I say, for I intend to give Mansoul another when this one is worn out for them.) For that, you must wholly and solely turn to, and rest on, the doctrine of the one who is your Teacher of the first rank. Yes, Mr. Conscience himself must not look for life from what he himself reveals; his dependence for that must rest on the other preacher’s doctrine. Let him also take care that he does not receive any doctrine, or point of doctrine, that is not passed on to him by his Superior Teacher, or that lies outside the bounds of his own proper knowledge.”

Now, after the Prince had settled things this way in Mansoul, he went on to give the elders of the corporation a necessary caution: how they should behave toward the high and noble captains he had sent or brought with him from his Father’s court.

“These captains,” he said, “love the town of Mansoul. They are picked men, picked out of a great many as the best suited and most faithful to serve in the wars of Shaddai against the Diabolonians, for the preservation of Mansoul. I charge you, therefore, you inhabitants of the now flourishing town of Mansoul, not to behave roughly or unkindly toward my captains or their men, for they are choice men, chosen out of many for your good. I say, I charge you not to treat them unkindly. For though they have the hearts and faces of lions whenever they are called out to engage and fight the King’s foes and the enemies of Mansoul, yet a little coldness shown them by Mansoul will make their faces fall, and will weaken them and take away their courage. So do not, my beloved, treat my valiant captains and courageous soldiers unkindly; but love them, nourish them, help them, and hold them close to your heart; and they will not only fight for you, but will drive from you all those Diabolonians who seek, and if possible will be, your utter destruction.

“If any of them, then, should at any time be sick or weak, and so unable to perform the service of love that with all their hearts they are willing to do (and will do, too, when they are well and healthy), do not slight them or despise them; rather strengthen and encourage them, even though they are weak and ready to die. For they are your fence and your guard, your wall, your gates, your locks, and your bars. And although when they are weak they can do but little, and need help from you rather than your expecting great things from them, yet when they are well you know what exploits and warlike feats they can and will perform for you.

“Besides, if they are weak, the town of Mansoul cannot be strong; if they are strong, then Mansoul cannot be weak. Your safety, therefore, lies in their health, and in your showing them your favor. Remember too that if they are sick, they catch that disease from the town of Mansoul itself.

“I have said these things to you because I love your welfare and your honor. So take care, my Mansoul, to be exact in all the things I have given you in charge; and that not only as a corporate town, toward your officers and guard and chief guides, but as a people, each one of whom depends for his own well-being on keeping the orders and commandments of his Lord.

“Next, my Mansoul, I warn you of something you need to be warned about, in spite of the reformation that has now been worked among you. So listen carefully to me. I am sure now, and you will know it hereafter, that there are still some Diabolonians left in Mansoul: Diabolonians who are sturdy and relentless, who even now while I am with you, and will more so when I am away from you, study, plot, contrive, invent, and join together in attempts to bring you to desolation, and so to a state far worse than the bondage of Egypt. They are the sworn friends of Diabolus, so look around you. In the past they used to lodge with their prince in the castle, when Incredulity was Lord Mayor of this town; but since my coming here they keep more to the outskirts and the walls, and have made themselves dens and caves and holes and strongholds there. That is why your work in this matter, Mansoul, will be all the harder: to seize them and put them to death according to my Father’s will. Nor can you rid yourselves of them entirely unless you pull down the walls of your town, which I am by no means willing you should do. Do you ask me, ‘What shall we do, then?’ Why, be diligent, and acquit yourselves like men. Watch their holes; find out their haunts; attack them, and make no peace with them. Wherever they haunt, lurk, or stay, and whatever terms of peace they offer you, abhor them, and all will be well between you and me. And so that you may better tell them apart from the natives of Mansoul, I will give you this brief list of the chief of them by name. They are these: Lord Fornication, Lord Adultery, Lord Murder, Lord Anger, Lord Lasciviousness, Lord Deceit, Lord Evil-Eye, Mr. Drunkenness, Mr. Revelling, Mr. Idolatry, Mr. Witchcraft, Mr. Discord, Mr. Rivalry, Mr. Wrath, Mr. Strife, Mr. Sedition, and Mr. Heresy. These, Mansoul, are some of the chief of those who will seek to overthrow you forever. These, I say, are the skulkers in Mansoul. But look well into the law of your King, and there you will find their features described, along with other marks of their character by which they can surely be known.

“These, my Mansoul (and I would gladly have you know it for certain), if they are allowed to run and range about the town as they please, will quickly, like vipers, eat out your insides; yes, they will poison your captains, cut the sinews of your soldiers, break the bars and bolts of your gates, and turn your now most flourishing Mansoul into a barren and desolate wilderness and a heap of ruins. So, to give you courage to seize these villains wherever you find them, I give to you, my Lord Mayor, my Lord Willbewill, and Mr. Recorder, with all the inhabitants of the town of Mansoul, full power and commission to seek out, to take, and to have put to death by the cross every Diabolonian of every kind, whenever and wherever you find them lurking within, or ranging outside, the walls of the town.

“I told you before that I had placed a standing ministry among you. Not that you have only these with you; for my first four captains, who came against the master and lord of the Diabolonians who was in Mansoul, can, and if need be and if they are asked, will not only instruct you privately but preach publicly to the corporation good and wholesome doctrine, such as will lead you in the way. Yes, they will set up a weekly lecture among you, Mansoul, or if need be a daily one, and will instruct you in such profitable lessons as will, if you heed them, do you good in the end. And take good care that you do not spare the men you have a commission to take and crucify.

“Now, as I have set the vagrants and runaways before your eyes by name, so I tell you this too: that some of them will creep in among you to deceive you, men who will seem to be, and in appearance are, very warm and zealous for religion. And if you do not watch, they will do you a mischief such as you cannot now imagine.
“These, as I said, will show themselves to you in a different color from those I described before. So, Mansoul, watch and be sober, and do not let yourself be betrayed.”
